Welcome to Nationhood
A multiplayer political simulation where you lead a political party, compete in elections, form governments, draft legislation, manage the economy, and navigate international diplomacy.
ALPHA · CRUCERA SHARD
Getting Started

Nationhood is a persistent political simulation. You lead a party in a real nation populated by other human and AI players, compete in elections, form governments, pass or block legislation, manage economies, and navigate diplomacy. Everything runs on a shared clock — the game advances on its own whether you're online or not.

1. Pick a nation

Your first decision is which nation to play in. On select-nation.html you'll see every nation grouped by continent (Crucera, Meridian, Al-Makir). Each card shows:

  • The nation's flag and short cultural blurb (e.g. "Dravka is analogous culturally to Albania")
  • Government type — Parliamentary Democracy, Presidential Republic, Semi-Presidential, Absolute Monarchy, or Constitutional Monarchy
  • Parliament size and number of active parties already in that nation

You can only found one party per user per nation. Pick a nation whose starting ideology profile, economy, and political vacancy match the kind of game you want to play. A crowded high-seat-count parliament plays very differently from a small monarchy with open slots.

2. Found your party

On the Create Party screen you set:

  • Name & abbreviation — used everywhere (bill authorship, vote tallies, event feeds)
  • Color — shown on your cards, dots next to your votes, and the parliament hemisphere chart
  • Logo — small emblem rendered on your faction card
  • Two ideology tags — drawn from the five axes (Liberty/Equality, Tradition/Progress, Security/Freedom, Globalism/Nationalism, Individualism/Collectivism). These anchor your party on the political map and shape voter bloc appeal.
  • Leader — auto-generated from the nation's name pool. You'll get a cultural-first-and-last name (e.g. Albanian for Dravka, Serbian for Vostia).

3. Starting resources

Every new party spawns with the same stack:

ResourceStarting valueWhat it does
Party Funds$1,000,000Cash for rallies, lawsuits, platform promises, campaign ads
Action Points (AP)5Political energy. You gain +5 AP every tick (+2 if your party is in government, ±1 from leader traits). AP accumulates — unspent points carry over. Most actions cost 1–4 AP.
Seats0Won at the next election. Until then you can't form government.
Approval Rating50How popular you are with voters. Moves with outcomes, promises, scandals.
Momentum0Short-term political energy. Rallies, statements, and positive events add; every tick burns some down.

4. Your first in-game hour

You don't have to be a master the day you sign up. A reasonable first session:

  1. Read the Home dashboard. It shows tick countdown, next election date, who's currently governing, and recent events in your nation.
  2. Visit the Government page. See current ministers, the standing PM (or President, or Queen/King), whether a coalition is formed, and what bills await royal assent if applicable.
  3. Scan the Bills page. Every pending bill shows who proposed it, the articles, the voting window. Even with 0 seats you can vote — your vote gets weighted by seat count when bills resolve, but casting a position signals your party's stance.
  4. Open Politics → Parties. Look at every party in your nation. Note who leads in seats, who shares your ideology, who would be a natural coalition partner.
  5. Adopt a platform. Politics → Parties → your card → "Adopt Platform". Each platform promises +20 on three stats and costs ~2 AP. First adopter gets +12 momentum; others get penalties if they copy you. You can hold three platforms at once with a 6-tick cooldown between adoptions.
  6. Glance at the Economy tab. Get familiar with your nation's GDP, debt, major industries, trade partners.

Common first-session mistakes

  • Burning all AP on turn 1. AP refills every tick; you don't need to spend all five in your first session. Save some for bills you didn't expect.
  • Adopting three platforms immediately. Platforms are commitments — you lose approval if the attached stats move the wrong way and don't recover at fulfillment tick. Start with one.
  • Ignoring coalition partners. Even at 0 seats you should identify who you'd ally with. After the first election, forming a coalition fast matters — a failed formation triggers snap elections.
  • Filing a no-confidence motion too early. It costs AP, has cooldowns, and usually fails without a majority of the opposition behind you.
How Ticks Work

Nationhood advances on a shared, shard-wide clock. Every tick (whose real-world interval is set per shard — production shards typically run on a multi-hour cadence) the game processes one in-game month. A 4-year parliamentary term is 48 ticks; a fast shard covers that in days, a slow shard in weeks.

What you see in the UI

  • Top-bar countdown. Shows how much real time remains until the next tick fires.
  • Current tick + in-game date. Displayed in the header. Tick 18 ≈ July 2001 on a January-2000 base.
  • AP gain. You gain +5 AP every tick (+2 if in the governing coalition, +1 if your leader has the Tireless Campaigner trait, −1 if Indecisive). AP accumulates tick-over-tick.
  • Fresh event feed. The Home tab's Events panel surfaces whatever fired this tick — passed bills, election triggers, diplomatic moves, crisis updates, news.

What happens under the hood every tick

When the clock hits zero, two server-side processors run back-to-back. You don't need to memorize the details, but knowing the order explains why effects sometimes arrive one tick later than expected.

advance-tick (nation + politics):

  • Scheduled elections fire; results compute; seats redistribute
  • Bills at end of voting window resolve — ordinary bills pass/fail, foundational bills check supermajority, confirmation bills confirm/reject ministers
  • Policy stat effects apply (one-shot effects fire once; ongoing effects increment until duration expires)
  • Active_laws momentum bonuses dispatch (e.g. Internet Sovereignty Act's per-tick coalition bonus)
  • Ministry crisis cards draw, resolve, or escalate
  • Trade flows recompute: domestic production, export capacity, import demand, actual trade volumes, price modifiers per sector
  • Tariff revenue posts to the treasury
  • Population grows; stats decay toward equilibrium; stat connections trigger across the stat graph
  • Agitator lawsuits advance through their milestone ticks; verdicts post to event_log
  • Protests and crises evolve
  • Momentum decays on every faction (unused momentum from rallies and press events fades if not spent)
  • Platform promises check their stat targets; fulfilled promises award approval, failed ones penalize
  • Coalition stability checks; governments can collapse if approval tanks below threshold
  • Treaties tick toward expiry or auto-renew

advance-corp-tick (corporation + economy):

  • Property effects: maintenance deducted, condition degrades, active refurbishments progress, buildings past completion snap to their refurbish_condition target
  • Corp monthly income: government contracts pay out, private operating revenue lands, loan interest/premium installments collect
  • Construction projects advance, consume materials, pay labor, risk events
  • Shipping routes generate, expire, or reassign; vessels leave port, transit, arrive, unload revenue
  • Finance: loan repayments collected, insurance premiums flow, equity dividends distribute
  • Reputation decay: 0.25/tick baseline, 1.0/tick if a corp has zero workforce

What this means for you

  • Submit actions before the tick fires. A bill proposal submitted 30 seconds before tick-end gets processed at that tick. One second after, it waits a full tick cycle. The countdown is your clock.
  • Expect delays. An enacted bill's stat effects start on the enactment tick, but the first tick's movement is often only partial. Look two or three ticks out to see the real shape.
  • You don't need to be online. AP refills, elections fire, and automatic processes run whether you're logged in or not. Adopt a platform, queue your rallies, log off, come back later.
  • Tick crunch time. Many players log in right before tick fires to submit last-minute actions. Opposition bills and rally timing often cluster at the end of a tick.
Your Party

You lead a political party inside one nation. Everything you do in the game flows through that party — winning seats, forming governments, proposing laws, campaigning, fundraising, coalition deals, diplomacy.

Your party's profile lives on the Politics → Parties tab. That's the single page where you can see your party's metrics and compare them to every rival party in the nation.

What the card shows you

Every party card has the same layout, yours or a rival's:

FieldWhat it means
Name & AbbreviationFull name and short form (e.g. "Social Democratic Front" → SDF). Used everywhere a party is referenced.
Party ColorThe color wash on your card and the dot next to your name in bills, votes, the parliament hemisphere, event feeds. Pick something distinctive — it's how people identify you at a glance.
LeaderThe face of your party. Shows name, age, and ideology. Leaders carry a trait that buffs or debuffs specific actions. Leaders age; when they retire or lose a no-confidence vote, you'll pick a successor from the candidate pool.
SeatsYour share of the legislature. Won through elections. Seats scale your voting power on bills, determine whether you can lead or support a coalition, and cap how much fundraising returns per cycle.
National Vote ShareYour percentage of the last election's votes (not seats). Can diverge from seats if the nation has entrenchment thresholds or seat bonuses.
ApprovalHow popular your party is with voters right now, 0–100. Drives your next election result more than any other stat. Rises from fulfilled platforms, successful rallies, positive crisis resolution. Falls from missed platform promises, failed lawsuits, scandals, and unpopular legislation you voted for.
MomentumShort-term political energy. Rallies, statements, press conferences, and winning news cycles add; every tick burns some off. A momentum spike right before an election can flip a result — momentum directly buffs turnout bonuses on your bloc.
IdeologyTwo ideology tags chosen at founding, plus a numeric position on five axes (see below). Voter blocs match against this; caucuses inside large parties track their own dominant axis against yours.
Coalition StatusGOVERNING-LEAD (your party holds the PM or presidency), GOVERNING-JUNIOR (you're in the coalition but not the lead), or OPPOSITION. Different statuses unlock different actions — only governing parties appoint ministers; only opposition parties can file no-confidence.
Ticks in PowerOn governing parties only. How long the current administration has lasted. Long tenure applies incumbency fatigue — a slow drip of approval loss that grows with time in power.
Party FundsCash for rallies, legal action, platform commitments, campaign advertising. Grown via fundraising (see below); drained by expensive actions.
Action Points (AP)Your per-tick action budget. Refills at the top of each tick. Most party actions cost 1–4 AP; some scale with polarization or escalation.

The five ideology axes

The game models political positioning on five symmetric 0–100 axes. Your party's position on each axis (set by your two chosen ideology tags and shifted by some actions) is compared against the electorate's ideological distribution.

Axis0 — Left pole100 — Right poleCore tension
Liberty–EqualityLIBERTYEQUALITYIndividual rights vs. collective fairness
Tradition–ProgressTRADITIONPROGRESSCultural conservatism vs. social reform
Security–FreedomSECURITYFREEDOMState protection vs. personal autonomy
Globalism–NationalismGLOBALISMNATIONALISMInternational integration vs. national sovereignty
Individualism–CollectivismINDIVIDUALISMCOLLECTIVISMPersonal self-reliance vs. communal structures

Each nation has its own electorate profile — a mean and variance on each axis, plus a salience weight telling you how much that axis matters in that nation's politics. Dravka cares about Tradition/Progress and Globalism/Nationalism (0.25 salience each); Progressive-leaning nations might invert that. Read a nation's electorate before you decide which ideology tags to pick.

Caucuses — internal wings of a dominant party

When you cross 50% of parliamentary seats, your party stops being a monolith. Internal caucuses activate — sub-factions inside your own party, each anchored to one ideology axis. Caucus count scales with seat share:

Seat shareCaucuses
50–59%2
60–69%3
70–79%4
80–100%5

Each caucus gets a name matched to its dominant axis wing — "Traditionalist Caucus" on the tradition pole of Tradition/Progress, "Reform Caucus" on the progress pole, "Security Hawks" vs "Civil Liberties Caucus" on Security/Freedom, etc.

Every caucus tracks a relationship score (0–100, default 65) against the party leadership. The score moves as you legislate:

  • +1 per favorable ideological article in a bill you pass that matches the caucus's axis
  • −20 when a bill opposed on that caucus's axis passes with your backing
  • +3 when you spend AP to whip a caucus into line on a critical vote
  • −2 per tick unconditional decay

At relationship ≤ 20 a caucus defects — its members split off to join an ideologically-compatible opposition party, taking their seats with them. A dominant party that ignores its caucuses can fragment within a few ticks.

Whipping costs AP (base 1 per whip, 2 for caucuses above 20% seat share). Used well, it's how you hold large coalitions together. Used carelessly, it burns relationship and triggers defections.

Party actions — what you can actually do

From your party card's action panel you can:

  • Hold a Rally — targets a voter bloc, consumes AP, returns momentum and approval. Diminishing returns if you repeat the same bloc; escalation cost climbs.
  • Press Conference — 1 AP; small momentum boost; escalation cost climbs with use.
  • Attack a rival party — AP cost scales with nation polarization. Outcome rolled from a weighted table: crit success, success, mixed, backfire, disaster. Winning damages target's approval; losing hurts you.
  • Fundraise — 5 tiers of diminishing returns per cycle:
    Use #Cash per seatMomentum cost
    1$5,000−1 per 10 seats
    2$4,000−1 per 8 seats
    3$3,000−1 per 6 seats
    4$2,000−1 per 5 seats
    5+$1,000−1 per 5 seats
  • Adopt a Platform — pick one of 16 platforms (Economic Reform, Social Justice, National Security, Anti-Corruption, Green Transition, etc.). Each promises +20 on three stats, penalizes three others, and takes up one of your three platform slots. Costs 2 AP. Momentum rewards the first mover and penalizes copies:
    • 1st adopter nationwide: +12 momentum
    • 2nd adopter: +6 to themselves, −6 to the first holder
    • 3rd adopter: +4 to themselves, −4 to each existing holder
    • 4th+ adopter: +2 to themselves, −2 to each existing holder
    6-tick cooldown between adoptions per party. Full details below.
  • File a Lawsuit (Agitator) — opposition tool. 8-tick timeline with milestone events. Outcome scales with the actual corruption/freedom-index growth since the current government took office; the worse their record, the stronger your case.

Platform promises

Adopting a platform is a public commitment with teeth. Each platform has:

  • Improve stats — 4–6 stats you promise to push up (e.g. Social Justice promises minimum wage, poverty rate, income inequality, social mobility, healthcare/education accessibility)
  • Worsen stats — 3–4 stats that are likely collateral damage (Social Justice hurts foreign investment, GDP growth, corporate tax revenue)
  • Tradeoff blurb — human-readable tension (e.g. "Capital flight risk. Foreign investors avoid high-tax environments. Growth may slow.")

Each platform occupies one of your three slots. Every tick, the tick processor checks whether the nation's stats are moving toward your promised targets. Fulfilled platforms award sustained approval; failed platforms (stats moving the wrong way) penalize you and your caucuses notice.

The coalition-formation UI on the Election tab shows every party's active platforms so other players can see what you've committed to before inviting you into a government.

Leader traits

Your party leader carries one trait_key from the leader_traits catalog. Each trait has:

  • Upside — a buff on one or more actions (e.g. −1 AP on rallies, +10% fundraising yield, better attack outcome odds)
  • Downside — a debuff to counter-balance (e.g. higher press-conference escalation, worse attack defense)

Traits are rolled at leader creation — both at founding and at each succession. You can see your leader's trait on the party card and its effects on the actions panel; some traits only apply in specific contexts (e.g. presidential traits only matter if your party is running a president).

Approval, embezzlement, and reputational damage

Two meters track the reputation layer of your party:

  • Approval — voter-facing, drives elections. Fast to move.
  • Embezzled Funds — a counter that increments when you take certain AP-cheap but legally-dubious actions. At threshold, triggers scandals; starts a consecutive embezzle ticks clock that makes lawsuits against you easier for opposition agitators.

Nation context & limits

Your party exists inside exactly one nation. You can't run candidates, propose bills, or hold ministries elsewhere. You can cooperate with parties in other nations via International Party Organisations (IPOs) on the Diplomacy page — an IPO lets member parties share momentum bonuses on aligned actions.

If your nation's government type changes mid-game (constitutional reform foundational law), your party's available actions shift with it:

  • Parliamentary → Presidential: no more coalition formation; you run a presidential candidate instead
  • Semi-presidential cohabitation: presidential-domain ministers (foreign, defense, trade) must come from the president's party even when the PM is opposition-led
  • Constitutional monarchy: hereditary Queen/King stays; PM is elected; your party can't contest the crown
  • Absolute monarchy: no elections; the monarch rules; your party's role becomes advisory or revolutionary

Read the Laws page before you consider voting yes on a government-type reform. The mechanics you're playing under can change overnight.

Government & Coalitions

After an election, parties must form a government:

  1. Any party can propose a coalition by selecting partner parties
  2. The coalition needs a majority of seats (more than half the legislature)
  3. Partners must accept the invitation and agree on ministry assignments
  4. The PM's party clicks Form Government to finalize

Being in government gives you:

  • Control of ministries (each with unique actions)
  • The PM can issue Public Addresses during crises

Not in government? You're the opposition. You can still vote on bills, organize protests, and run for election.

Bills & Legislation

Bills are how you change your nation. The lifecycle:

  1. Draft — propose articles with policy effects, tax changes, or funding adjustments
  2. Committee — other parties can co-sponsor or add amendments
  3. Floor Vote — send to the floor; all parties vote for 6 ticks
  4. Passed/Failed — majority wins. Passed bills take effect immediately.

Bill Types

  • Standard bills — enact policies that change nation stats over time
  • Tax reform — adjust income, corporate, or sales tax rates
  • Funding bills — change ministry institution funding levels
  • Repeal bills — reverse an active law
  • Foundational laws — change seat counts, term lengths, or government structure (requires 2/3 majority)
  • No Confidence — dissolve the current government and trigger new elections
Elections & Campaigning

Elections are the single moment that resets the political map. You go into one with a particular seat count, approval, and ideological position; you come out with a new seat count that sets the terms for every policy fight until the next election.

Election schedule

  • Parliamentary elections fire on a fixed cadence set by your nation's constitution (typically every 4 game years, 48 ticks). The "Next Election" countdown on the Home / Dashboard tab shows ticks remaining.
  • Presidential elections run separately in presidential and semi-presidential systems, on their own schedule.
  • Snap elections can be triggered by a successful Vote of No Confidence, a failed government-formation deadline, or certain constitutional-reform bills.
  • You don't have to do anything for a scheduled election to fire. The game runs it automatically when the tick arrives — but the political work happens in the ticks leading up to it.

How seats get allocated

Seats aren't awarded purely by vote share. Behind the scenes the game scores every party against every voter bloc, then sums to allocate seats. Four factors drive your result:

FactorWeightWhat it is
Party Approval40%Your approval going into the election. The single biggest number.
Momentum30%Short-term boost from rallies, statements, and events in the final stretch. Fades fast if you don't keep it topped up.
Ideology Alignment30%How closely your positions on the five ideology axes match what voter blocs want.

Voter blocs

Each nation has a demographic breakdown — urban professionals, working class, rural traditionalists, religious conservatives, progressive youth, etc. Each bloc weights parties differently based on ideology.

You don't target blocs directly. You position your party's ideology on the five axes, and alignment does the work. Use Statement and Platform Promise actions to nudge your axes toward the blocs you want to win.

Campaigning

Campaigning happens every tick, not just during a campaign window. The sooner you start, the more approval and momentum you'll have banked by election day.

The main campaigning tools live on the Actions tab:

  • Fundraise — accumulates party funds, which pay for the expensive actions below. Escalates in size the more ticks you do it in a row, so steady fundraising beats sporadic.
  • Rally — spends party funds for a targeted approval and momentum spike. Highest impact per fund-unit; best used shortly before an election.
  • Statement — cheap ideological move that shifts one of your five axes and nudges approval/momentum. Use regularly to keep your positioning sharp.
  • Platform Promises — commit to stat targets (e.g. "reduce poverty by 5"). Fulfilled promises pay approval dividends; unmet promises punish you. Treat them as binding campaign pledges.
  • Lawsuits — opposition-only. Target a rival party with a legal action. Wins hurt the target's approval; losses hurt yours. Legally risky, politically loud.

Full mechanics of each action are covered in the Actions section. For election week specifically, the pattern most players converge on is: fundraise aggressively for 4–8 ticks, then spend it all on rallies and platform promises in the final 2–3 ticks before the vote.

Incumbency effect

If you've been in government for a while, expect a steady approval decay. Voters get bored with the same administration. The "Ticks in Power" counter on your card tracks this — every tick above the threshold chips your approval.

Conversely, opposition parties get a small tailwind the longer a specific government has been in office. You don't have to do anything to get it — just exist and stay positioned for the day voters want change.

After the election

When the election resolves:

  1. Seats are recalculated for every party.
  2. The current government dissolves.
  3. A government-formation window opens. Parties propose coalitions, assign ministries, and the lead party clicks Form Government.
  4. If no coalition forms by the deadline, a snap election is called and the process repeats.
  5. Once a government forms, your coalition status is set (GOVERNING-LEAD / GOVERNING-JUNIOR / OPPOSITION) and your available actions change accordingly.

Special elections

  • Vote of No Confidence — legislators file a motion to dissolve the current government. If it passes with a majority, the government falls and a snap election or formation attempt follows.
  • Failed Formation — if no coalition forms within the deadline after an election, a snap election fires and seat counts reset.
  • Constitutional Reform — certain foundational bills (e.g. switching from Parliamentary to Presidential) trigger a reset election so the new system starts fresh.
The Economy

Every nation has a full economic simulation:

  • GDP — grows or shrinks based on gdp_growth stat
  • Budget — revenue (taxes + trade + oil) minus expenditures (ministry costs + debt service)
  • Debt — deficits accumulate as debt. High debt erodes credit and locks out borrowing.
  • Trade — nations automatically import and export based on their stats and sector strengths
  • Inflation — rises with spending and money supply, falls with austerity

Visit the Economy tab and click ? Guide for detailed breakdowns of each sub-tab.

Ministries

Coalition parties are assigned ministries. Each ministry has unique actions that draw from the ministry's discretionary fund:

MinistryKey Actions
HealthcarePharmaceutical Regulation (increase/decrease)
LaborStrengthen Unions / Deregulate Labor
TransportationPublic Transit Investment, Road Maintenance
EducationWorkforce Development, Curriculum Orientation
DefenseMilitary actions (coming soon)
ForeignDiplomacy actions (on the Diplomacy page)
FinanceDebt Restructuring

Ministry actions have escalating costs on repeated use, and their effects scale down with diminishing returns.

Diplomacy

Diplomacy requires holding the right role:

  • Foreign Minister — manage relations, propose major initiatives
  • Minister of Trade — negotiate trade agreements, impose tariffs
  • Head of Government — state visits, war & peace (coming soon)

Visit the Diplomacy tab and click ? Guide for the full diplomacy guide covering trade agreements, initiatives, IPOs, and more.

International Party Organisations (IPOs)

IPOs are cross-nation alliances of like-minded parties. Create or join one from the Diplomacy → IPO subtab. Costs are paid in cash from your party funds.

  • Solidarity Fund — members contribute cash quarterly for collective actions
  • Rallies — boost approval for member parties
  • Symposiums — shift a nation's ideology
  • Back-channels — secretly transfer cash between members
  • Voting — democratic decision-making within the org
Protests & Crises

Opposition parties can organize protests to pressure the government. Protests have tiers:

  • Tiers 1-5 — one-time effects (approval loss, unrest). Higher tiers require higher turnout scores.
  • Tier 6 — requires 1+ active crisis. Creates an ongoing crisis with per-tick stat penalties. Fizzles after 1-6 ticks.
  • Tier 7 — requires 3+ active crises. The most severe protest crisis. Fizzles after 1-12 ticks. Government must meet a specific demand.

The PM can use Public Address (40% T6 / 15% T7 chance to resolve), the Interior Minister can Enforce Public Order (33% resolve, 66% escalate), or the PM can declare a National Emergency (guaranteed resolution, severe stat penalties).

Tips & Strategy

For New Players

  • Fundraise steadily rather than sporadically — the escalating tier means consecutive ticks compound
  • Co-sponsor bills from other parties to build relationships for coalition negotiations
  • Check the Economy tab regularly — a deficit that spirals into a debt crisis is hard to recover from
  • Your party's ideology matters for elections — be consistent with what your voters want

For Government Parties

  • Use ministry actions every few ticks — they're powerful and you lose access if you lose power
  • Watch government approval — it's computed from minister performance and events
  • Fund your institutions — underfunded ministries trigger crises

For Opposition

  • Vote strategically on floor bills — don't just vote no on everything
  • Organize protests when the government is vulnerable (low approval, active crises)
  • Build ideological appeal with voter blocs you can win
  • Join IPOs to coordinate with allies in other nations
